title: How Dictators Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how dictators work: the origin of the word "dictator" in ancient Rome (emergency office with six-month limits), how Sulla, Julius Caesar, and Napoleon consolidated power, the difference between authoritarian and totalitarian regimes, cults of personality, the ways dictators come to power (elections, power vacuums, coups), coups and military juntas, sham elections, how dictatorships end, the decline of dictatorships after the Cold War, and a run of odd anecdotes about dictators (Kim Jong Il's film kidnapping, the Beatles in the Philippines, Idi Amin's "White Man's Burden," Gaddafi's female bodyguards, Hitler's synthetic comforter). The episode closes with a listener mail segment about rescued pets and a sign-off.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and dictators' common traits
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by noting they have not lived under a dictatorship and that dictatorships were the norm for much of history. They discuss the word 'dictator', that leaders rarely call themselves that, and that North Korea's leadership is shrouded in uncertainty. They note dictators usually do not take power through free elections.

segments.title: Origin of the dictator office in ancient Rome
segments.summary: The hosts trace the word to the Roman Republic, where two consuls were equal, and in emergencies one was appointed dictator with broad power for up to six months, immune from criminal liability, but barred from leaving Italy, changing public money use, and so on. Some dictators overstayed. Sulla was appointed dictator without a term limit, changing the pattern.

segments.title: Julius Caesar, Napoleon and benevolent dictators
segments.summary: Caesar fled Sulla, returned after his death, became dictator through a coup, and was popular with the lower classes, forgiving debts and improving infrastructure, but was assassinated by the Senate elite. The hosts discuss the subjective idea of a benevolent dictator. Napoleon rose during a state of emergency, became consul for life and then emperor, balancing the budget and writing civil law, while controlling the press and using spies.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break; the hosts mention a sidebar on Emperor Palpatine they agree to skip.

segments.title: Authoritarian vs. totalitarian regimes and cults of personality
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish authoritarian regimes, led by a single leader without effective checks, from totalitarian regimes that control politics, economy, media and social life. Totalitarian states use secret police and encourage citizens to spy on each other. Dictators foster a cult of personality with posters and statues; Turkmenbashi's golden statue that rotated to face the sun is discussed.

segments.title: How dictators end and how they come to power
segments.summary: The hosts describe the downfall of dictators, often through illness or capture, citing Lenin, Stalin, Castro, Saddam Hussein, and Manuel Noriega. They note Hitler was appointed chancellor legitimately, and Saddam rose from vice president. They conclude that the route to power varies, and depends on the person and circumstances.

segments.title: Coups, military juntas and sham elections
segments.summary: A coup is described as a smaller operation by military elites, not a mass uprising, and can be bloodless or violent; Pinochet's coup in Chile is cited as an example of a coup where the former president was executed. A military junta is a committee-led dictatorship, with Fiji and Thailand given as examples. Dictators sometimes hold farcical elections, with Saudi Arabia's 2005 local elections, which excluded women, discussed.

segments.title: Decline of dictatorships, foreign policy and odd dictator anecdotes
segments.summary: The hosts note dictatorships are believed to be declining worldwide, with the Cold War's superpower propping up of dictators and its end leading to fewer dictatorships. They discuss a Reason magazine article on US foreign policy toward autocracies. Then they recount odd stories: Kim Jong Il kidnapping director Shin Sang-ok to make films, Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos's invitation to the Beatles, Idi Amin's chair carried by white men, Gaddafi's female bodyguards, and a reported Hitler-era synthetic comforter.

segments.title: Listener mail: rescued kitten and ferrets
segments.summary: Chuck corrects an earlier mix-up about 'pump and dump' in the baby-animal bottle-feeding episodes. A listener named Chris writes about his sister rescuing ferrets and a kitten that grew up ungrateful.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact information and sign off.
